title: The El Niño that's 'off the charts'
credits: Photos: Anders Marlowe, Mike Erskine, Chris Gallagher, NOAA, Saikiran Kesari / Unsplash · Map: Natural Earth
lines: The United Nations has issued an unusual warning: this year's El Niño could be the strongest ever recorded.
El Niño is a natural warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean, and it shifts weather patterns around the whole planet.
The head of the World Meteorological Organization, Celeste Saulo, says it is literally off the monitoring charts used for the past four decades.
Sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific could run three point eight degrees above average, between November and January.
The event is expected to peak around December, but its effects could last well into twenty twenty-seven.
The UN's aid chief, Tom Fletcher, called it a wrecking ball for Latin America, Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
That means droughts in some regions, and floods and cyclones in others.
Fletcher has released fifty million dollars for eleven of the most exposed countries, including Chad, Ethiopia, Somalia and El Salvador.
He warned that the humanitarian system cannot cope on its own, and countries must act early.
El Niño usually returns every two to seven years, and lasts nine to twelve months.
The last one helped make twenty twenty-four the hottest year on record.
